architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added From<&[T]> trait implementations for Line and Text to enable slice-based construction
architecture_decisions.rationale: The existing API only supported construction from Vec<T> and single elements. Adding slice support provides more flexibility for users who have data in slices (e.g., array slices, slice views) without requiring them to allocate a new Vec. This follows Rust's convention of providing From implementations for common collection types.
alternatives_considered: Only supporting Vec<T> and requiring users to call .to_vec() on slices
Using AsRef<[T]> instead of &[T] as the parameter

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Used generic bounds T: Into<Span> + Clone for Line and T: Into<Line> + Clone for Text with appropriate lifetime annotations
architecture_decisions.rationale: The Clone bound is necessary because we need to iterate over the slice and convert each element. Since we're taking a reference to the slice (&'b [T]), we need to clone each element before converting it. The Into<T> bound ensures type safety while maintaining flexibility - it allows conversion from any type that can become a Span/Line (String, &str, styled spans, etc.). The lifetime annotations ('a, 'b) properly handle the relationship between the source slice's lifetime and the resulting Line/Text's lifetime.
alternatives_considered: Using T: AsRef<Span> instead of T: Into<Span>
Requiring T: Copy instead of T: Clone (too restrictive)
Using owned values instead of references (would require allocation)

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Maintained the same pattern as existing From implementations by using ..Default::default() and collecting into the appropriate field
architecture_decisions.rationale: The implementation follows the established pattern in the codebase: create a new struct with default values, then set the spans/lines field by mapping and collecting the input. This ensures consistency with other From implementations (like From<Vec<Span>>) and makes the code predictable for maintainers. Using ..Default::default() ensures other fields (like alignment, style) are properly initialized.
alternatives_considered: Creating a completely new initialization pattern
Manually setting all fields instead of using default

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added comprehensive test cases covering different slice types and ranges
architecture_decisions.rationale: Tests verify that the implementation works correctly with: 1) slices of Spans, 2) slices of &str, 3) slices of String, 4) different slice ranges (start..end, start..). This ensures edge cases like empty slices are handled (via collect() on empty iterator) and that the Clone requirement works correctly. The tests mirror existing test patterns in the module.
alternatives_considered: Relying on existing tests for Vec<T> implementations

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Updated documentation comments to mention the new slice conversion capability
architecture_decisions.rationale: The documentation for Line and Text now includes mentions of From<&[Into<Span>]> and From<&[Into<Line>]> respectively. This helps users discover the feature through IDE tooltips and documentation. The wording matches the existing documentation style.
alternatives_considered: Using different wording that doesn't match existing style

implementation_summary:
The implementation adds slice-based construction capabilities to the Line and Text types in the ratatui library by implementing From<&[T]> trait conversions. This enhancement provides more ergonomic APIs for users who have data in slice form, allowing them to create text elements without manual iteration or unnecessary allocations.

The key design decision was to use generic bounds T: Into<Span> + Clone for Line and T: Into<Line> + Clone for Text, which provides maximum flexibility while maintaining type safety. The Clone bound is necessary because we're working with references to slice elements, and we need to clone each element before converting it. This approach maintains consistency with existing From implementations in the codebase, using the same ..Default::default() pattern and collecting results into the appropriate fields.

The changes integrate seamlessly with the existing codebase by following established patterns. The implementations handle empty slices correctly (producing empty collections), and the comprehensive test suite ensures proper behavior with various input types and slice ranges. This enhancement aligns with Rust's convention of providing From implementations for common collection types, making the library more intuitive for users familiar with Rust's standard library patterns.
